title: First words
goal: Greet people politely, say yes and no, thank someone, apologise and ask how someone is.
intro:
Welcome to Hindi! In this unit you'll learn the words you'll use every single day: hello, yes, no, thanks, sorry. You'll also meet the most important social idea in Hindi grammar: there are **three words for 'you'**, depending on how respectful or close you are.

Don't worry about reading the script fast yet — use the romanization, listen, and repeat out loud.

vocab.en: hello; goodbye (respectful, any time of day)
vocab.note: Said with palms pressed together. Works for hello and goodbye.
Common in speeches, TV news and with elders.
Also negates verbs: मैं नहीं जानता 'I don't know'.
Add to yes/no (जी हाँ, जी नहीं) or after a name (शर्मा जी) for respect. On its own it means 'yes?' or 'pardon?'.
Formal/written. In speech many people say शुक्रिया or simply 'thank you'.
Everyday word, shared with Urdu.
Mostly on signs and in formal requests. In speech, politeness comes from the verb form (कीजिए, दीजिए) and ज़रा.
f · माफ़ी चाहता हूँ 'I apologise' (formal)
English loan, extremely common in everyday speech.
ठीक है 'OK, alright' is one of the most used phrases in Hindi.
As a reply: 'OK' (falling tone) or 'Really?' (rising). Changes to अच्छी/अच्छे with gender/number.
Default for strangers, elders, anyone you're unsure about. Takes plural verb forms.
For friends, younger people, siblings, partners.
Very close friends, small children, God, or to be rude. Avoid as a learner.
Agrees like an adjective: कैसा (m. sg), कैसी (f.), कैसे (m. pl / respectful).
At the start of a sentence it just turns it into a yes/no question.
m · क्या हाल है? 'How are things?'
Comes AFTER the word it refers to: मैं भी 'me too'.
Usually pronounced 'bohot'.
m · आपका स्वागत है 'welcome' (also used as 'you're welcome').
m/f · plural दोस्त. Also मित्र mitra (formal).
मिलकर milkar 'having met'.
f · often pronounced khushī.
Calls attention or shows surprise. Informal.
Dramatic — used for long partings and in songs. Day to day say नमस्ते, फिर मिलेंगे or 'bye'.
English loan; very common, informal. ओके 'OK' and हेलो 'hello' (on the phone) are also used.

phrases.en: How are you? (polite, to a man)
How are you? (polite, to a woman)

phrases.note: Also to get attention. Informal: माफ़ करना.

phrases.en: Nice to meet you. (lit. having met you, happiness happened)
See you again. (lit. we'll meet again)

grammar.title: Word order: the verb comes last
grammar.body:
English says *I am fine*; Hindi says **मैं ठीक हूँ** — literally 'I fine am'. Hindi is a **subject–object–verb** (SOV) language: the verb (here हूँ 'am') goes at the end, and everything else comes before it.

Subject – (object / description) – verb
मैं – ठीक – हूँ

Questions use the same order. You can turn a statement into a yes/no question just by raising your voice at the end, or by putting **क्या** at the front. Question words like कैसे 'how' usually go right before the verb.

examples.en: Are you OK? (kyā you fine are)

grammar.title: Three ways to say 'you': आप, तुम, तू
grammar.body:
Hindi chooses its 'you' by **respect and closeness**, and the verb changes with it:

**आप** *āp* — respectful: strangers, elders, teachers, shopkeepers, in-laws, anyone in a formal setting. Verb: **हैं** *haiṃ*.
**तुम** *tum* — familiar: friends your age, younger relatives, children, partners. Verb: **हो** *ho*.
**तू** *tū* — intimate or rude: best friends, small children, prayers. Verb: **है** *hai*.

When in doubt, use **आप** — nobody is offended by too much respect. Adding **जी** makes almost anything more polite: जी हाँ 'yes (respectfully)', and after a name, रवि जी 'Ravi-ji'.

Note also that कैसा 'how' changes its ending: कैसे for men (and for the respectful आप), कैसी for women.

examples.en: How are you? (familiar, to a man/boy)
How are you? (familiar, to a woman/girl)
How are you? (intimate, to a close male friend)

dialogue.title: Meeting a neighbour
dialogue.setting: Ravi meets his new neighbour, Mrs Sharma, on the stairs in the morning.

lines.speaker: Ravi
lines.native: मैं ठीक हूँ, शुक्रिया। और आप?
lines.roman: maiṃ ṭhīk hūṃ, shukriyā. aur āp?

lines.speaker: Mrs Sharma
lines.native: मैं भी ठीक हूँ। आपसे मिलकर ख़ुशी हुई।
lines.roman: maiṃ bhī ṭhīk hūṃ. āpse milkar xushī huī.
lines.en: I'm fine too. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: Ravi
lines.native: जी, मुझे भी। आपका स्वागत है!
lines.roman: jī, mujhe bhī. āpkā svāgat hai!

lines.speaker: Ravi
lines.native: अरे, माफ़ कीजिए, मैं जल्दी में हूँ।
lines.roman: are, māf kījiye, maiṃ jaldī meṃ hūṃ.
lines.en: Oh, sorry, I'm in a hurry.

culture: **नमस्ते** with palms pressed together and a slight nod is safe with everyone. You'll also hear greetings tied to community and region: **अस्सलाम अलैकुम** *assalām alaikum* among Muslims (reply **वालैकुम अस्सलाम**), **सत श्री अकाल** *sat shrī akāl* among Sikhs, and **राम-राम** or **जय श्री कृष्ण** in villages and among older Hindus. Touching an elder's feet is a sign of deep respect in families. Among close family and friends, saying 'thank you' too often can sound distant — warmth is shown by actions instead. Young urban speakers mix English freely: *hi, bye, sorry, thank you, OK* are all perfectly normal Hindi today.
